# The buy button
Source: https://docs.litium.dev/accelerators/mvc-accelerator/develop/the-buy-button

How the buy button is implemented in Litium Accelerator.

The buy button is used to add a product to a cart. It works asynchronously, which means the page does not have to reload and the mini cart is reloaded automatically. The buy button:

* Can be used in MVC Razor view.
* Should work asynchronously so the page does not reload.
* Should update the mini cart or any other component that needs to reload.
* Can add one or many quantities.
* Should show a notification message when an item is added to the cart.

Here we will go through the code required and show how it meets these requirements.

## Render the buy button on the server side

On the server side, the buy button is created by calling the extension method of MvcHtmlString, located in ProductItemViewModelHtmlExtensions.cs:

```cshtml theme={null}
@Html.BuyButton(model => model.ProductItem, cssClass: "product-detail__buy-button", isBuyButton: true)
```

Where model.ProductItem should return the Litium.Accelerator.ViewModels.Product.ProductItemViewModel.

We can build the ProductItemViewModel from a variant, by using the ProductItemViewModelBuilder. Remember to import the extension namespace:

```cshtml theme={null}
@using Litium.Accelerator.Mvc.Extensions
```

The buy-button parameter is used to decide if clicking the button will add a product to the shopping cart, or simply navigate to the product's page.

The server side renders an HTML tag named buy-button, with some data attributes which are used later when creating the React component:

```html theme={null}
<buy-button data-article-number="636743401924888880-02423006_L" data-css-class="button buy-button product-detail__buy-button" data-quantity-field-id="41fa735e-0473-4238-82f6-68b3d0e3c7ae">Add to car</buy-button>
```

## Render a buy button in React

A built-in BuyButton component should be used like this:

```jsx theme={null}
import BuyButton from './Components/BuyButton';

<Provider store={store}>
    <BuyButton {...{ label, articleNumber, quantityFieldId, href, cssClass }}/>
</Provider>
```

This is explained as follows:

* store: the Redux store object. The store object can be found in the index.js file, as well as in window.\_\_litium.store.
* label: the label of the button.
* articleNumber: the article number should be added to the cart when the button is selected.
* quantityFieldId: the unique id of the quantity field to get the quantity value.
* href: in case articleNumber is not available, href will be used as a hyper link for the buy button.
* cssClass: the css class for the button.

## Cart.service.js, Cart.action.js and Cart.reducer.js

The add() function in Cart.service.js sends a POST request to /api/cart/add (CartController.cs) with the article number and quantity. A new cart object will be sent back by CartController. This object is then stored in the Redux state named cart by using receive action. The reducer that handles this action is Cart.reducer.js. All components that consume this state will be updated, for example the mini cart.

## CartController

When the buy button is clicked, a POST request is sent to the Add action of the CartController. The controller then adds the article to the cart, and returns the new cart using CartViewModelBuilder.

The Add action is decorated with the ApiValidateAntiForgeryToken, to prevent cross-site request forgeries. HTTP requests sent from the client have the token in the header, with RequestVerificationToken as the key. This is done automatically in the HTTP service, of Client\Scripts\Services\http.js. So, we do not have to worry about this when sending an HTTP request from the client side, as long as we use the HTTP service:

```javascript theme={null}
import { get, post, put, remove as httpRemove } from '../Services/http';
```

The server side action, however, needs to be decorated with ApiValidateAntiForgeryToken (Litium.Accelerator.Mvc.Attributes.ApiValidateAntiForgeryToken). It is used for WebAPI actions, while System.Web.Mvc.ValidateAntiForgeryToken is used for MVC actions.

By looking at the Network tab of Google Chrome's DevTools, we can see the request with the RequestVerificationToken header, and the actual payload. Switching to the Preview tab, we can also see the Cart object that is returned from the CartController. This is the object that we store into the Cart state of Redux, and MiniCart.js component presents this data to the UI.

<img alt="DevTools showing the request and cart response" />


# Overview
Source: https://docs.litium.dev/accelerators/mvc-accelerator/develop/the-checkout/overview

This is a description of how the checkout process is built. Both from a back-end and front-end perspective.

The checkout page in Litium Accelerator is an MVC page, while the actual checkout form is built as a React component. We will go through which part does what and how they interact with each other.

## Configuration

The checkout page is configured as follows:

1. Navigate to the Website area in back office.
2. Go to Start and use Checkout page template to create the page.
3. Then create a terms-and-conditions page, so that a link there can be included on the checkout page. It can have any template but let us use the article page template.
4. Edit the checkout page and set a link to the terms-and-conditions page:

<img alt="Checkout terms configuration" />

5. Create a page using the order confirmation template.
6. Navigate to Settings, select Websites > Websites and choose the website where the checkout and order confirmation pages you created belong:

<img alt="Website settings" />

7. Edit the checkout page and order confirmation page properties, so they point to the pages we created above. Make sure they are published and activated for the current channel. The checkout page should now be ready to use.
8. Litium Accelerator can be configured to display checkout forms targeting B2C or B2B customers, or both. To configure this, set the Allow private or company customers (B2C or B2B) options in the website configuration.

## Checkout page

The checkout page is built of several different parts:

* Index Razor view.
* Checkout MVC controllers.
* Checkout WebAPI controller.
* Checkout component, written in React.
* Checkout action and reducer, written in Redux.

Let us take a closer look at them:

### Index Razor view

The view is located under Litium.Accelerator.Mvc\Views\Checkout\Index.cshtml. It contains an empty DIV tag, with checkout as id so that the React Checkout component will be loaded to that position.

It also contains the script to set the Redux state for the checkout page. The state is built by the CheckoutViewModelBuilder and set to window.\_\_litium.preloadState, which is the global JavaScript variable. This preload state is the initial state, which we use when [Redux store](https://redux.js.org/api/createstore) is created. That means the Checkout component has the data right when the page is loaded, which avoids unnecessary requests. The Checkout component load part is done in Litium.Accelerator.Mvc\Client\Scripts\index.js:

```jsx theme={null}
if (document.getElementById('checkout')) {
    const Checkout = Loadable({
        loader: () => import('./Components/Checkout'),
        loading: () => <div></div>,
    });
    ReactDOM.render(
        <Provider store={store}>
            <Checkout />
        </Provider>,
        document.getElementById('checkout')
    );
}
```

Note that the Checkout component is loaded on demand. It is not bundled in the app.min.js file, to reduce the size of the main JavaScript file. We use the Checkout component only in the checkout page and does not need it for other pages.

### Checkout controllers

There are two checkout controllers, one MVC and one WebAPI. They handle different requests:

* Checkout MVC controller: serves the request to render the checkout page, using the Index Razor view above. It also serves responses from payment providers. For example, a user who selects DIBS as payment option will be redirected to the DIBS's website to enter a credit card. The user will then be redirected back to the website, either by completing the payment or by cancelling it. Those requests are served by this controller, with the HandleResponse and HandleCancelResponse methods.
* Checkout WebApi controller: serves AJAX requests made by the client code, for example, to place an order or change the delivery/payment method. It receives the CheckoutViewModel and returns the same model. All actions are decorated with the ApiValidateAntiForgeryToken to prevent cross-site request forgeries. This is similar to the configuration in CartController for the [Buy button](/accelerators/mvc-accelerator/develop/the-buy-button).

When a user selects a payment option on the checkout page, an AJAX request is sent to the checkout WebAPI controller, to action SetPaymentProvider. If the selected provider has a payment widget, a PaymentWidgetResult will be sent to the client to render the payment widget. For example, if a user selects Klarna Checkout, a Klarna Checkout widget will be rendered in the browser. If DIBS is selected, no widget must be rendered since the user is redirected to DIBS's payment page instead.

Please read more about [working with payment providers here](/accelerators/mvc-accelerator/develop/the-checkout/payment-and-delivery-providers).

Place order request is processed in the PlaceOrder action of the WebApi checkout controller, where most of the logic is done in CheckoutServiceImpl.cs. Thanks to the framework, most of the important checkout logic is done in the cart located there.

### React Checkout component

The React Checkout component takes responsible for rendering the checkout form. It consists of the cart detail section, the address form, delivery and payment options, and the order detail section. If the payment provider has a payment widget, it will be rendered in React too.

There are some components:

* cart details - Cart.js
* address form for private customers - Checkout.PrivateCustomerInfo.js
* address form for business customers - Checkout.BusinessCustomerInfo.js
* delivery options - Checkout.DeliveryMethods.js
* payment options - Checkout.PaymentMethods.js
* order details section - Checkout.OrderInfo.js and Checkout.OrderNote.js

Each component is responsible for rendering and processing a small and specific part of the checkout form. Then the Checkout.js component connects them all together, adds the validation.

### Checkout action and reducer

The actual logic is placed in Checkout.action.js and Checkout.reducer.js. While Checkout.reducer.js is very "thin" - it simply takes the data in an action and merges it into the corresponding state - Checkout.action.js is considered "fat". The action is responsible for sending requests to the WebApi controller, process the request and [dispatch](https://redux.js.org/api/store#dispatch) the action to the reducer, to trigger the state change. The examples below show how the actions set payment provider and place order work:

```javascript theme={null}
export const setPayment = (systemId) => (dispatch, getState) => {
    dispatch({
        type: CHECKOUT_SET_PAYMENT,
        payload: {
            selectedPaymentMethod: systemId,
        }
    });
    const { payload } = getState().checkout;
    return put('/api/checkout/setPaymentProvider', payload)
        .then(response => response.json())
        .then(result => {
            dispatch(loadCart());
            dispatch(setPaymentWidget(result.paymentWidget));
        })
        .catch(ex => dispatch(catchError(ex, error => submitError(error))))
}
```

This is what happens when a user selects a payment option:

* A CHECKOUT\_SET\_PAYMENT action is dispatched to set the selected payment method Id for the Redux state. The CheckoutPaymentMethods component will set the corresponding radio button as checked when the state is updated.
* A PUT request is sent to the SetPaymentProvider action of the checkout WebAPI controller. It has the checkout state as payload, which is the CheckoutViewModel. Note that the checkout state has the selectedPaymentMethod, so the WebApi controller has the Id of the payment method the user has selected.
* The checkout WebApi controller changes the payment method, sets PaymentWidget to CheckoutViewModel, if any, and returns CheckoutViewModel to the client.
* When the checkout action receives the response, it does two things: first it reloads the cart by calling the loadCart() function, to get the latest Cart object. This is to show the new price, because a payment fee might be added. Then it calls setPaymentWidget to dispatch the CHECKOUT\_SET\_PAYMENT\_WIDGET action. The checkout reducer then updates the state to store the payment widget.

Now, depending on what we have in the payment widget, PaymentWidget will either render it or just an empty block. PaymentWidgetResult has the Id, which is the Id of the payment provider, and ResponseString is the response from the payment provider. Klarna Checkout, for instance, would have KlarnaCheckout as Id, and the [HtmlSnippet](https://developers.klarna.com/api/#checkout-api-create-a-new-order) as ResponseString. We use this ResponseString to render the Klarna Checkout widget.

This action is called when the Place order button is clicked:

```javascript theme={null}
const _submit = (url, model, dispatch) => {
    return post(url, model)
        .then(response => response.json())
        .then(result => {
            dispatch(submitDone(result));
            if (result.redirectUrl) {
                window.location = result.redirectUrl;
            }
        })
        .catch(ex => {
            if (ex.response) {
                ex.response.json().then(error => {
                    dispatch(submitError(error));
                    dispatch(submitDone(null));
                });
            } else {
                dispatch(submitError(ex));
            }
        })
    ;
}
```

The url parameter has /api/checkout as its value, and the model parameter has the Checkout state as payload, which is the CheckoutViewModel. It sends a POST request to the PlaceOrder action of the checkout WebAPI controller, which returns the new CheckoutViewModel. If the model has the RedirectUrl, the browser will then be redirected to the new URL. This is the case when a user selects a "Redirect payment" like DIBS, and will be redirected to DIBS's payment page. Or, if the order is placed, the RedirectUrl will guide the browser to navigate to the order confirmation page.

If an error occurs, it will be handled in the catch() function. The error can be a validation error or other error types. Checkout.js will catch the error, show the error message, and scroll the browser to the incorrect field if it is a validation error. See the useEffect hook of handling errors in Checkout.js for detail.

## Validation

Client side validation is done with [Yup](/accelerators/mvc-accelerator/develop/front-end-coding/working-with-javascript). Different validation schemas are defined for private and business customers.

## Payment and delivery methods

Payment providers and methods can be downloaded as Litium Add-ons. Please read more about [payment providers here](https://docs.litium.com/add-ons/add-ons-as-extensions/payment-extensions). Always consult the respective payment providers regarding installation and configuration.

To enable and show the payment/delivery methods in the checkout page. Please read more about [working with payment providers here](/accelerators/mvc-accelerator/develop/the-checkout/payment-and-delivery-providers).

<img alt="Payment and delivery methods" />


# Ability to define customer type in checkout
Source: https://docs.litium.dev/accelerators/mvc-accelerator/develop/the-checkout/payment-and-delivery-providers/ability-to-define-customer-type-in-checkout

How to define a customer type in the checkout.

This is useful when you need to divide the checkout flow into one for private persons (B2C) and one for companies or organizations (B2B). It will usually also have an impact on the flow in any payment widget used on the checkout page.

### How to define customer type in Checkout

Litium has two types of customers as defined by CustomerType

* Person
* Organization

The property CustomerType in CheckoutFlowInfo is used to decide which checkout flow should be used for the checkout page. The Litium Accelerator sets the value for the CustomerType based on the CheckoutMode value in website settings.

<img alt="Checkout customer type setting" />

In CheckoutController.cs

```csharp theme={null}
private CheckoutFlowInfo GetCheckoutFlowInfo()
        {
            var websiteModel = _requestModelAccessor.RequestModel.WebsiteModel;
            var checkoutPage = websiteModel.GetValue<PointerPageItem>(AcceleratorWebsiteFieldNameConstants.CheckoutPage);
            var checkoutModeInt = websiteModel.GetValue<int>(AcceleratorWebsiteFieldNameConstants.CheckoutMode);
            var checkoutPageUrl = GetAbsolutePageUrl(checkoutPage);

            return new CheckoutFlowInfo
            {
                CustomerType = ToCustomerType((CheckoutMode)checkoutModeInt),
                CheckoutPageUrl = checkoutPageUrl,
                TermsUrl = GetAbsolutePageUrl(checkoutPage?.EntitySystemId.MapTo<PageModel>().GetValue<PointerPageItem>(CheckoutPageFieldNameConstants.TermsAndConditionsPage)),
                ReceiptPageUrl = GetAbsolutePageUrl(websiteModel.GetValue<PointerPageItem>(AcceleratorWebsiteFieldNameConstants.OrderConfirmationPage)),
                CancelPageUrl = checkoutPageUrl
            };

            static CustomerType? ToCustomerType (CheckoutMode checkoutMode) => checkoutMode switch
            {
                CheckoutMode.PrivateCustomers => CustomerType.Person,
                CheckoutMode.CompanyCustomers => CustomerType.Organization,
                CheckoutMode.Both => null,
                _ => throw new NotSupportedException("The checkout mode " + checkoutMode + " is not supported")
            };
        }
```


# Overview
Source: https://docs.litium.dev/accelerators/mvc-accelerator/develop/the-checkout/payment-and-delivery-providers/overview

Enable, configure and edit the payment and delivery methods.

Litum has several pre-built payment providers which are built as apps. Refer to these two articles for more information regarding Litium App:

* [Litium Apps](/apps/litium-app)
* [App installation flow](/apps/litium-app)

The checkout page has a list of payment and delivery methods for a visitor to choose from:

* Checkout.DeliveryMethods.js declares the component that shows the list of delivery options.
* Checkout.PaymentMethods.js is responsible for the payment options.

When a visitor selects an option, a PUT request is sent to the CheckoutController WebApi controllers. They are SetPaymentProvider for payment options and SetDeliveryProvider for delivery options. The controller then sets the selected option and returns the payment widget if the current payment option wants to render one.

## Enable payment and delivery methods

To enable and show the payment and delivery methods on the checkout page, we need to configure the channel and set up different payment/delivery methods for different countries.

1. Click on the cogwheel to navigate to the back office settings.
2. Select Globalization > Channels > the channel you want to modify.
3. Switch to Countries and configure the country as well as the corresponding payment/delivery methods there.

<img alt="Channel configuration" />

## Configure a payment account

Each payment provider needs a different configuration. In general, they all require the merchant to sign up for an account and then apply it in the configuration file. Please check the configure section of [Litium Apps](/apps/litium-app) to see how this is done, for example, [Configure Klarna](/apps/klarna-payment).

## Edit a payment or delivery method

<img alt="Payment and delivery methods list" />

Payment and delivery methods can be configured in terms of:

* name
* description
* icon
* cost
* VAT

Open the settings by clicking on the cogwheel in back office, navigate to Globalization > Channels, switch to Countries tab, and select an item to edit:

<img alt="Payment configuration" />


# Change country in cart
Source: https://docs.litium.dev/accelerators/mvc-accelerator/develop/the-shopping-cart/change-country-in-cart

How to change country in cart, and its effects.

In the Litium accelerator, changing country on the checkout page will affect the cart context, such as currency code, the product price, discount information, delivery/payment methods.

Logic of updating country can be found in: Litium.Accelerator.Mvc\Controllers\Api\CheckoutController.cs - SetCountry action

**Select country**

```csharp theme={null}
await cartContext.SelectCountryAsync(new SelectCountryArgs
{
    CountryCode = model.SelectedCountry
});
```

**Select delivery option**

```csharp theme={null}
var selectShippingOptionArgs = new SelectShippingOptionArgs
{
    ShippingOptionId = model.SelectedDeliveryMethod
};
await cartContext.SelectShippingOptionAsync(selectShippingOptionArgs);
```

**Select payment option**

```csharp theme={null}
var selectPaymentArgs = new SelectPaymentOptionArgs
{
    PaymentOptionId = model.SelectedPaymentMethod
};
await cartContext.SelectPaymentOptionAsync(selectPaymentArgs);
```


# Display mini cart
Source: https://docs.litium.dev/accelerators/mvc-accelerator/develop/the-shopping-cart/display-mini-cart

The mini cart is displayed in the top-right corner of all pages.

The mini cart is shown on all pages, where it always stays at the top-right corner. Here is what happens when a page, for example the start page, is loaded:

* \_Layout.cshtml is used to render the page. It invokes the Index action of the ClientContextController, which calls ClientContextViewModelBuilder to build the CartViewModel, and renders the partial view ClientContext.cshtml.

<img alt="Render ClientContext" />

* ClientContext.cshtml renders a script block that sets the cart data for the preloadState. Here is the source of the start page, where we can see the output script block:

<img alt="Preload state script output" />

* Header.cshtml renders an empty DIV tag with miniCart as the id.

<img alt="Header renders miniCart div" />

Here it is the server that builds the CartViewModel, sets it as the value of window.\_\_litium.preloadState.cart and renders an empty DIV tag with miniCart as the id.

This is what happens when the browser renders the page:

* index.js is executed first. It constructs Redux's store with the preloadState, so that we have the cart's data in the state, ready to use.

<img alt="Create Redux store with preload state" />

* index.js also finds the DIV tag with miniCart as the id and boots up the MiniCart component.

<img alt="Mini cart rendered in UI" />


# How cart object is stored
Source: https://docs.litium.dev/accelerators/mvc-accelerator/develop/the-shopping-cart/how-cart-object-is-stored

The cart object is stored in the CartContext.

The CartContext can be accessed via an extension of HttpContext or CartContextAccessor which are located under Litium.Sales.

```csharp theme={null}
using Litium.Sales;

public class SampleController : ApiControllerBase
{
    private readonly CartContextAccessor _cartContextAccessor;

    public SampleController(CartContextAccessor cartContextAccessor)
    {
        _cartContextAccessor= cartContextAccessor;
    }

    public IActionResult GetViaHttpContext()
    {
        var cartContext = HttpContext.GetCartContext();
        return Ok(cartContext.Cart);
    }

    public IActionResult GetViaAccessor()
    {
        var cartContext = _cartContextAccessor.CartContext;
        return Ok(cartContext.Cart);
    }
}
```


# Modify the shopping cart
Source: https://docs.litium.dev/accelerators/mvc-accelerator/develop/the-shopping-cart/modify-the-shopping-cart

The shopping cart can be updated by adding or removing items, by changing the quantity, or removing items.

To understand how it works and update the cart, [please read the buy button article](/accelerators/mvc-accelerator/develop/the-buy-button).

There is a section in the checkout page where detailed information of a cart is displayed, and where a visitor can change the quantity or remove items. This area is rendered by Cart.js. Actions update, coming from Cart.action.js, is called in that case.

```javascript theme={null}
export const update = (rowSystemId, quantity) => (dispatch) => {
    return put(`/api/cart/update`, { rowSystemId, quantity })
        .then(response => response.json())
        .then(cart => dispatch(receive(cart)))
        .catch(ex => dispatch(catchError(ex, error => loadError(error))))
        ;
}
```

The first parameter is the id of the order row. The second parameter is the quantity. If it is zero, the item will be removed from the cart.

The update action of CartController.cs would then be invoked. It returns the new cart model so that the client components can update their data to show the new information.


# Overview
Source: https://docs.litium.dev/accelerators/mvc-accelerator/develop/the-shopping-cart/overview

How the shopping cart works in Litium Accelerator.

The shopping cart in Litium Accelerator is built as a React component. It displays the CartViewModel, built by the CartViewModelBuilder. You can also build the shopping cart in another library or framework.

To understand how this works, let us look at the components that are needed:

**Back end:**

* CartController: a WebAPI controller to communicate with the React component.
* CartViewModelBuilder: a model builder that is part of the Business Logic Layer (BLL). Please read more about the [BLL](/accelerators/mvc-accelerator) here.
* CartContext: to handle the shopping experience with providing the Cart and CheckoutFlowInfo.
* ClientContextViewModelBuilder: to build the client context view model, which contains the cart's data. This client context is returned to the client via the DOM content, so that the cart component can use it. Please read more about it in the article about the [architecture of Litium Accelerator](/accelerators/mvc-accelerator/develop/accelerator-architecture).

**Front end:**

* MiniCart.js: the mini cart component that is shown in the top-right corner of every page.
* Cart.js: the cart component that is shown on the checkout page.
* Checkout.js: the checkout component that contain Cart.
* Cart.action.js: the Redux action for the cart.
* Cart.reducer.js: the Redux reducer for the cart.


# Install
Source: https://docs.litium.dev/accelerators/mvc-accelerator/install-litium-accelerator

Installation instructions for Litium accelerator.

Follow the steps below to install the latest version of the Accelerator. Please see the release notes for the [latest version here](/accelerators/mvc-accelerator/release-notes).

### Before you start

Before Litium Accelerator is installed you need to set up the [Litium NuGet feed](/platform/get-started/litium-packages).

Also, set up Elasticsearch, Redis, and Kibana. Please see the [setup instructions here](/platform/get-started/shared-dependencies).

Use a [version control system](/accelerators/mvc-accelerator/upgrade-and-maintenance) for easy upgrades of Litium Accelerator.

### Install the template package

The Accelerator template package is a pre-created package.

Installation of the template package is only needed the first time the version is created.

Only one version of the template package can exist at the same time.

1. Open Powershell command prompt
2. Install the template pack with

```powershell theme={null}
dotnet new install "Litium.Accelerator.Templates"
```

After the template is installed, a list of available templates is shown.

<img alt="Install template package" />

*Note: To update the template to a later version, you should run the installation command again.*

If you want to install a specific version of the template you need to append the version number to the template name separated by two colons (::) example for template for the 8.0.0 version

```powershell theme={null}
dotnet new install "Litium.Accelerator.Templates::8.0.0"
```

## Install and run Litium Accelerator

1. Open the Powershell command prompt in the folder where the Accelerator should be installed.
2. Install the Litium Accelerator with the following command.

```powershell theme={null}
dotnet new litmvcacc
```

To include the Storefront API in the accelerator installation you need to add the --storefront-api to the commando

```powershell theme={null}
dotnet new litmvcacc --storefront-api
```

<img alt="Install accelerator command" />

During the creation of Litium Accelerator, the restore of projects and installation of litium-db tool are performed.

If the installation is performed without errors, continue to step 3.

Manually restore the project's dependencies

```powershell theme={null}
dotnet tool restore
dotnet restore
```

Manually install litium-db tool

```powershell theme={null}
dotnet new tool-manifest
dotnet tool install Litium.Application.Migrations
```

Please find more information about database management and [how to install specific versions of the db-tool here](/platform/get-started/developer-tools/db-tool).

3. Setup the database with help of the litium-db tool. Using the command (*Note! A empty database must exist before the command can run*)

```powershell theme={null}
dotnet litium-db update --connection "Pooling=true;User Id=user;Password=secret;Database=litium8;Server=127.0.0.1;TrustServerCertificate=True"
```

*Remember to replace the settings in the connectionstring for your database.*

4. Config your Litium Accelerator installation.

See [.Net configuration](http://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/configuration/), where you should put common non secret settings for the project (appSettings.json, appSettings.Development.json, and appSettings.Production.json), [user-secrets should be used for development configuration and local secrets](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/security/app-secrets?view=aspnetcore-5.0\&tabs=windows).

### Optional: Build the client project (only if you are modifying client resource files)

The Litium Accelerator comes with pre-built client resource files, so you do not have to build them yourself.

However, if you have modified client resources under any project, then you need to build the project. Here is how to do it:

1. Make sure that you have [NPM](https://www.npmjs.com/get-npm) and [Yarn](https://yarnpkg.com/lang/en/docs/install/) installed and in the path.
2. Execute BuildClientProjects.bat file.

*Note:*

* If you are building Litium.Accelerator.FieldTypes, the output folder is Litium.Accelerator.FieldTypes\dist. Build the Litium.Accelerator.FieldTypes.csproj after building client resources to embed the script in the assembly.
* If you are building Litium.Accelerator.Mvc, the output folder is Litium.Accelerator.Mvc\UI. If you update only js, scss or cshtml files, then you do not need to build Litium.Accelerator.Mvc.csproj. Note that you still need to build client resources when you update js files.
* If you are building Litium.Accelerator.Email, the output folder is Litium.Accelerator.Email\dist. By default, ConfirmationEmail.html is copied to Litium.Accelerator.Mvc\Views\Email and renamed with .cshtml as extension. In case you want to automatically copy more files when building the project, modify gulpfile.babel.js file to add more files to be copied in the copy function.

## Create your accelerator website

1. In Visual Studio, go to Solution Explorer and select the Litium.Accelerator.Mvc project. Context-click and select Set as StartUp project.
2. Start the accelerator with the Start without debugging option in the Debug menu. This will open a web browser with the port number. Type "litium" after the port number to display the login page for the Litium back office.
3. Log in as a user with System All permissions. Please read more about [how to log in here](/platform/get-started/create-admin-user-and-log-in). Example "[https://localhost:5001/litium](https://localhost:5001/litium)"
4. Open the settings by clicking the cogwheel in the upper right corner. In the left panel, expand the node Deployment where you will find the accelerator.

<img alt="Deployment node in settings" />

5. Click on the accelerator to install.
6. Enter a name and a domain name for the Accelerator website.

<img alt="Deploy accelerator dialog" />

7. Click the Import button and wait for a message confirming that the installation was successful.

Note that an active internet connection is needed to download the installation package.

Your accelerator website has now been created.

This means that the following items are also created:

* A folder in Media for the Accelerator media files.
* An assortment for the Accelerator categories and products.
* A price list.
* An inventory.
* The default B2B buyer roles Order approver and Buyer.

## Secure connection (SSL)

Every page should use a secure connection. By setting the HSTS (Http Strict Transport Security) for the domain name, we force the website to use HTTPS instead of HTTP. To configure HSTS, navigate to **Settings** > **Globalization** > **Domain names**, select a domain name, click **Edit** and then choose to edit **HSTS max age** to a value greater than 0.

[From Qualys](https://blog.qualys.com/vulnerabilities-threat-research/2016/03/28/the-importance-of-a-proper-http-strict-transport-security-implementation-on-your-web-server) it is advisable to assign the max-age directive's value to be greater than 10368000 seconds (120 days) and ideally to 31536000 (one year). Websites should aim to ramp up the max-age value to ensure heightened security for a long duration for the current domain and/or subdomains.


# MVC accelerator
Source: https://docs.litium.dev/accelerators/mvc-accelerator/overview

What it is and how it works.

The MVC accelerator consists of technical solutions, know-how, and methods that can get a project up to speed quickly.

Every e-commerce project needs components like product presentation with filters, checkout, customer registration, and, mobile version. Litium accelerator provides them as a package, so they do not have to be figured out for every new project. It is a flexible solution that can be customized and developed in terms of functionality and design.

A customer solution can be [extended further by add-ons](https://docs.litium.com/resources/download-add-ons), which are defined functionalities that can be added to the accelerator. The illustration below shows the context of the accelerator.

<img alt="MVC accelerator concept" />

## Basic structure

The accelerator is built using .NET MVC and React components for front-end, and a Business Logic Layer for business rules.

<img alt="MVC accelerator architecture" />

### Business Logic Layer

The Business Logic Layer (BLL) contains all logic, from the different field templates to the logic for how a product search is executed. The BLL does not depend on the technology of the MVC or web API. It will produce a view model that can be used in the rendering layer to produce the content for a visitor. The view model can be used in both the MVC and web API rendering layer.

### MVC rendering layer

The MVC rendering layer is a "thin" layer acting as a bridge between the visitor request and the BLL. The result from the BLL is transformed with the MVC view engine to create the HTML output that will be returned to the visitor.

### Web API rendering layer

The web API rendering layer is a "thin" layer acting as a bridge between the BLL and the functions executed with JavaScript in the browser. The result from the BLL is transformed into JSON, which is processed with the caller method in the browser.

<img alt="MVC accelerator rendering layers" />

## Technical frameworks

The MVC accelerator uses the responsive framework [Foundation by Zurb](http://foundation.zurb.com/) together with [React](https://reactjs.org/).

A layout (flex-grid) with media queries from Foundation by Zurb is used. There are also custom-built styles on top of Foundation, specifically for the Accelerator. The custom-built styles use SCSS files and the BEM naming convention.

To speed up the development of front-end components like menus, shopping cart, and product filtering, React can be used to organize the code and make it cross-browser compatible. React is also useful to build advanced front-end functions that communicate with the back end via a web API.

All front-end assets, like style sheets and JavaScript, are processed with Webpack. During build, it will compile, analyze, and bundle the different assets into optimized files.

The MVC accelerator provides extensions to the platform, which can also be extended:

* *Litium.Accelerator.FieldTypes*: to add custom field types to the platform. Please read more about [how to create custom field types](/platform/guides/data-modelling/how-to-create-custom-field-types), [how to create custom panel](/platform/guides/back-office-ui-extensions-how-to-create-a-custom-panel), [how to create custom widgets](/platform/areas/dashboard/how-to-create-custom-dashboard-widgets), and [how to use dialogs](/platform/guides/back-office-ui-extensions-display-dialogs).
* *Litium.Accelerator.Administration.Extensions*: provides a set of custom Setting pages for the platform. Please read more about [how to create custom Setting page](/platform/guides/back-office-ui-extensions-how-to-create-a-custom-page-under-settings).
* *Litium.Accelerator.Administration.Deployment*: the Accelerator Deployment screen is built as a separated NuGet package. The UI is also written in Angular. The NuGet package is installed by default, which is shipped also with the source code. The customize the Deployment screen, extract the NuGet package *Litium.Accelerator.Administration.Deployment* file, as it is a zip file. The source code is located under the *Src* folder. Remove the NuGet package from *Litium.Accelerator.Mvc* project and add the Source code project to the solution. Please read more about [how to create custom Setting page](/platform/guides/back-office-ui-extensions-how-to-create-a-custom-page-under-settings) to understand how the Deployment page was built.

Please read more about the [MVC accelerator architecture](/accelerators/mvc-accelerator/develop/accelerator-architecture).


# Upgrade and maintenance
Source: https://docs.litium.dev/accelerators/mvc-accelerator/upgrade-and-maintenance

Manage your Litium solution with source control, for easy upgrades.

This guide will help you to manage your Litium solution with an easy upgrade to the [Litium Accelerator's latest version](/accelerators/mvc-accelerator/release-notes) even if you started to modify the code in your solution. It will provide you with information about:

* The importance of using source control
* Solution maintenance
* Upgrading the Litium Accelerator

## The importance of using source control

We strongly recommend that you use a source control system to maintain the source files of the Litium project. Without one you will have difficulties maintaining the source of the Litium solution.

There are several online services that provide source control possibilities, such as GitHub, Azure DevOps, Bitbucket, and Gitlab.

The most adapted source control system today is Git, and you have several services that you can use if you do not want to install and maintain the source control system inside your organization.

This guide is written in a general-purpose and using the Git terminology, but the concept should work with any source control system.

## Solution maintenance

Maintaining the Litium Accelerator solution with source control, and making it easy to update to a later version, is done with a branching strategy. By using a branching strategy, you get a solution where it is easy to apply the changes made between the Litium Accelerator versions.

In this guide, the branch name main is used as the default branch that all developers are working towards.

* Create your source control repository and name the branch as main.

From the main branch, you should make a new branch. Making this branch as early as possible from the main branch will make it easier to apply new versions of Litium Accelerator.

* Create and switch to a new accelerator-vanilla branch.

```bash theme={null}
git checkout -b accelerator-vanilla
```

The accelerator-vanilla branch will be the truth of Litium Accelerator and this branch should only contain the changes that are from the Litium provided package for Litium Accelerator.

* Add the Litium Accelerator source into the branch.
* Commit with a message "Accelerator X.Y.Z".

```bash theme={null}
git add -A
git commit -m "Accelerator X.Y.Z"
```

Note: If other changes are done in this branch, the later update steps will not work.

* Switch back to your main branch and merge the changes from the accelerator-vanilla branch.

```bash theme={null}
git checkout main
git merge accelerator-vanilla
```

Now the main branch is ready for your project changes.

## Upgrading the Litium Accelerator

When a [new version of the Litium Accelerator](https://docs.litium.com/accelerators/mvc-accelerator/release-notes-mvc-accelerator) has been released it is time for the solution to get the changes in the Litium Accelerator package.

Please read The importance of using source control and Solution maintenance carefully, before you get started.

### Preparations

* Switch branch to your accelerator-vanilla branch.

```bash theme={null}
git checkout accelerator-vanilla
```

Now the solution is reverted to how everything was from the beginning.

* Delete all files that were added by the Litium Accelerator package. If this branch was created with a nearly empty version of files, it is easy to clear files out from the directory.
* Add all files from the new Litium Accelerator package.

```bash theme={null}
git add -A
```

* Commit with a message "Accelerator X.Z.Z".

```bash theme={null}
git commit -m "Accelerator X.Z.Z"
```

The commit that is created contains the difference between Litium Accelerator X.Y.Z and X.Z.Z.

* Switch back to main branch.

```bash theme={null}
git checkout main
```

* Create and switch to a new branch merge-accelerator-x-z-z.

```bash theme={null}
git checkout -b merge-accelerator-x-z-z
```

The source control system is now ready to apply the changes that have been made between the Litium Accelerator versions.

### Merge

Now we merge Litium Accelerator changes into the current version of the solution.

* Merge the accelerator-vanilla branch into the current merge-accelerator-x-z-z branch.

```bash theme={null}
git merge accelerator-vanilla
```

The merge of the Litium Accelerator changes can end in two different situations. We prefer the second, but the first also commonly occur.

1. Merge conflict.
   * Resolve merge conflicts.
   * Make a merge commit "Merge Accelerator X.Z.Z".

```bash theme={null}
git commit -m "Merge Accelerator X.Z.Z"
```

2. Everything can be merged automatically, and a new merge-commit will be created.

If changes have been made in the same rows of code in both the Litium Accelerator default version and in the project solution, the merge cannot successfully complete, and a conflict is created.

In this case, you need to solve the merge conflicts manually and due to the nature of the source control system, you only need to solve the changes which have happened in the solution after the initial Accelerator version and the upgraded Accelerator version.

If the changes are in the Accelerator and the solution has not changed the same lines the source control system will manage to merge the changes automatically.

Ensure that the merge-accelerator-x-z-z branch is building and working as expected before merging the branch back to main to avoid that solution is broken and can't be delivered to the test and production environment.

* Switch branch to main and merge the merge-accelerator-x-z-z.

```bash theme={null}
git checkout main
git merge merge-accelerator-x-z-z
```


# Get started
Source: https://docs.litium.dev/accelerators/react-accelerator/get-started

System requirement, installation and configuration instructions for React accelerator.

## System requirements

* [Node.js](https://nodejs.org/en/) 20 or later version.
* Yarn 1.22 is recommended. Using npm might lead to some issues. ([1](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/issues/72204)) ([2](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/issues/72026))
* Litium 8.19 or later version including Storefront API, see [Litium Empty template](/platform/get-started/install-empty-litium) for installation.

<Note>
  Installation based on Litium Mvc Accelerator have conflicting fields, field templates and settings and can't be run in the same installation without manual modification of templates to contain fields and settings for both the Mvc Accelerator and React Accelerator as well that all field template that exist for Mvc Accelerator also need to exist in React if the page should work. This setup is not recommended for easy maintenance.
</Note>

## Install the template package

The React accelerator template package is a pre-created package. Installation of the template package is only needed the first time the version is created. Only one version of the template package can exist at the same time.

1. Open Powershell command prompt
2. Install the template package with:

```shell theme={null}
dotnet new --install "Litium.Accelerator.React.Templates"
```

## Install the React accelerator

1. Open the Powershell command prompt in the folder where the template should be installed.
2. Install the React accelerator with the following command:

```shell theme={null}
dotnet new litreactacc
```

3. Install dependencies:

```shell theme={null}
yarn install
```

## Install Storefront CLI

Litium.Storefront.Cli is a command line tool which is used to forward requests to React accelerator site. To install the tool, execute the following command in Powershell command prompt:

```shell theme={null}
dotnet tool update -g Litium.Storefront.Cli
```

For more information regarding Storefront CLI, please click [here](/platform/get-started/developer-tools/storefront-cli#gen-excel).

## Configure the React accelerator

Prepare the environment with an .env.local (or .env.test.local if running tests) file that contains the following information to run the development environment:

```
# The domain name for you Litium platform installation.
RUNTIME_LITIUM_SERVER_URL=https://litium.localtest.me:5001

# If you using self-signed certificate for the Litium platform
# you may also need to add the following line to turn off certificate validation.
NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED="0"
```

## Import definitions

To ensure the React accelerator functions correctly, you need to import default data such as fields and field templates using the Storefront CLI. Go to the Back-office, navigate to the Customers module to create an administrator user with Content permisison for all modules and then use the account to perform the import by executing:

```shell theme={null}
litium-storefront definition import --file "../Litium.Storefront/litium-definitions/**/*.yaml" --litium https://localhost:5001/ --litium-username admin --litium-password Password!
```

For more info, please check the [Storefront CLI](/platform/get-started/developer-tools/storefront-cli#gen-excel).

## Import website texts

Storefront uses the website texts to populate values for translatable fields. To have these texts populated in the default installation, the default website text value need to be imported using WebsiteText import function (Setting / Websites / Texts / Import). The text file, which is in Excel format, can be generated using the Storefront CLI. For more info, please check the [Storefront CLI](/platform/get-started/developer-tools/storefront-cli#gen-excel).

## Configure SMTP server

This section describes how to configure a SMTP server for the Litium React accelerator.

**SMTP configuration**

You can setup an SMTP server to send emails for example order confirmations to customers. The SMTP settings can be updated in .env.local (or .env.test.local if running tests) file that contains the following information to run the development environment:

```
RUNTIME_SMTP_HOST: the host name or ip-address of smtp service.
RUNTIME_SMTP_PORT: the port of the smtp service.
RUNTIME_SMTP_SECURE: if set to True, the TLS communication should be used for smtp service communication.
RUNTIME_SMTP_AUTH_USER: the user name for the smtp service.
RUNTIME_SMTP_AUTH_PASS: the password for the smtp service.
```

**A sender email address is required to send emails from the application**

* In Litium backoffice, go to Setting > Globalization > Channels and double-click your channel
* Find the Send email address setting and add a valid email as value
* Click Save

This section provides an overview of how to send emails in the React Accelerator.

* Litium uses React Email to create new email templates and then converts them into HTML email templates.
* To send emails in the React accelerator, Litium utilizes the Nodemailer SDK.
* In the React accelerator, an API route is defined in `src/app/api/email/[[...slug]]/route.ts` with the endpoint specified as `api/email/[[...slug]]`. The `slug` is used to handle requests with different translation cases. For instance, you can have an endpoint like `api/email` where the slug value is undefined, or `api/email/language` where the slug value is an array \[language].
* Once you have created this endpoint, you can send it to the backend using a `createCheckoutSession` mutation. In the Litium platform, this endpoint can be called when an order is confirmed.

```javascript theme={null}
await createCheckoutSession({
    orderConfirmedUrl: `${host}/api/email${pathname}`,
})
```

## Configure Litium for an external storefront

Open the appsettings.json and add Storefronts configurations below the Websites element.

```json theme={null}
{
  "Litium": {
    "Websites": {
      "Storefronts": {
        "headless-accelerator": {
          "host": "https://localhost:3001/"
        }
      }
    }
  }
}
```

* headless-accelerator is the name on the installation
* host is the url where this accelerator is found. The address should point to the litium storefront proxy

Then open Litium back office to configure:

* Edit the website. On the tab for settings, select the external storefront that was configured in appsettings.
* On the website page, ensure that every setting in the Properties tab is completed with information, and that published pages are used for page pointer fields.
* Add a domain name named localhost, then navigate to the working channel, add this domain in Domain URL tab.

## Start a development environment

Run the following command to ensure the proxy is active:

```shell theme={null}
litium-storefront proxy --litium https://litium.localtest.me:5001/ --storefront http://localhost:3000/
```

* port - represents the port the proxy should listen to
* litium - url to the litium installation
* storefront - url to the storefront application

Execute yarn dev to start the development environment. After that, open [https://localhost:3001/](https://localhost:3001/) with your browser to see the outcome. You can start editing the page by modifying files under the app folder. The page will auto-updates as you make changes.

```

```

# How to query and mutate data
Source: https://docs.litium.dev/accelerators/react-accelerator/how-to-query-and-mutate-data

This guide explains how to query and mutate data in the Litium React accelerator, a Next.js application that uses Apollo Client for GraphQL operations.

## Querying data in Server components

Server components run on the server and have access to Next.js headers. Use queryServer from *services/dataService.server.ts*

**Function signature**

```typescript theme={null}
async function queryServer(options: {
  query: DocumentNode;           // GraphQL query (required)
  client?: ApolloClient;         // Custom client (optional)
  url?: string;                  // Current page URL (optional, defaults to headers)
  variables?: any;               // Query variables (optional)
  fetchPolicy?: FetchPolicy;     // Cache policy (optional, defaults to 'no-cache')
}): Promise<any>
```

**Basic example**

```typescript theme={null}
import { gql } from '@apollo/client';
import { queryServer } from 'services/dataService.server';

async function getContent({ params }: { params: any }) {
  return await queryServer({
    query: GET_CONTENT,
    variables: {
      first: 10,
      after: '0',
    },
    url: params.slug?.join('/') ?? '/',
  });
}

const GET_CONTENT = gql`
  query GetContent {
    content {
      ... on ContentConnection {
        nodes {
          id
          name
        }
      }
    }
  }
`;
```

## Querying data in Client components

Client components run in the browser and require the `'use client'` directive. There are two methods for querying data in client components.

**Method 1: Using useStorefrontQuery hook**

A React hook that wraps Apollo's useQuery with automatic context URL injection. This provides a declarative, reactive approach.

**Hook implementation**

```typescript theme={null}
import { OperationVariables, TypedDocumentNode } from '@apollo/client';
import { useQuery } from '@apollo/client/react';
import { DocumentNode } from 'graphql';
import { HeaderKeys } from 'utils/constants';

/**
 * A wrapper around Apollo's useQuery that automatically sets the context URL
 * from window.location for Litium Storefront queries.
 */
export function useStorefrontQuery<
  TData = any,
  TVariables extends OperationVariables = OperationVariables
>(query: DocumentNode | TypedDocumentNode<TData, TVariables>, options?: any) {
  const contextUrl = typeof window !== 'undefined' ? window.location.href : '';

  const mergedOptions = {
    ...options,
    variables: {
      [HeaderKeys.CacheUrl]: contextUrl,
      ...options?.variables,
    },
    context: {
      ...options?.context,
      headers: {
        ...options?.context?.headers,
      },
    },
  };

  return useQuery<TData, TVariables>(query, mergedOptions);
}
```

**Basic example**

```tsx theme={null}
'use client';
import { gql } from '@apollo/client';
import { useStorefrontQuery } from 'hooks/useStorefrontQuery';

export default function MyComponent() {
  const { data, loading, error, refetch } = useStorefrontQuery(GET_DATA, {
    variables: {
      id: '123',
    },
  });

  if (loading) return <div>Loading...</div>;
  if (error) return <div>Error: {error.message}</div>;

  return (
    <div>
      <h1>{data?.content?.name}</h1>
    </div>
  );
}
```

**Method 2: Using queryClient function, from services/dataService.client.ts**

A versatile async function for executing GraphQL queries in Client Components. This is a general-purpose method that can be used in various scenarios throughout your application.

**Function signature**

```typescript theme={null}
async function queryClient(options: {
  client?: ApolloClient;         // Custom client (optional, defaults to global)
  query: DocumentNode;           // GraphQL query (required)
  url?: string;                  // Page URL (optional, defaults to window.location.pathname)
  host?: string;                 // Host (optional, defaults to window.location.host)
  variables?: any;               // Query variables (optional)
  context?: any;                 // Apollo context (optional)
  fetchPolicy?: FetchPolicy;     // Cache policy (optional)
}): Promise<any>
```

**Basic example**

```typescript theme={null}
'use client';
import { gql } from '@apollo/client';
import { queryClient } from 'services/dataService.client';

async function fetchData() {
  const data = await queryClient({
    query: GET_PRODUCTS,
    variables: {
      first: 20,
      after: '0',
    },
  });
  return data;
}

const GET_PRODUCTS = gql`
  query GetProducts($first: Int, $after: String) {
    products(first: $first, after: $after) {
      nodes {
        id
        name
      }
    }
  }
`;
```

**Note: Context URL for Cache Isolation**

The `[HeaderKeys.CacheUrl]` variable is used to ensure proper cache isolation per page, preventing cache collisions where different pages might incorrectly return the same cached content.

**Automatic Support for All Client Query Methods**

Both `queryClient()` and `useStorefrontQuery()` automatically inject the `[HeaderKeys.CacheUrl]` variable into your query variables. No manual configuration is required.

**Code implementation**

* queryClient

```typescript theme={null}
// From: services/dataService.ts

export async function query({ client, query, url, host, variables, ... }) {
  return await execute({
    queryFn: async (client, context, cacheUrl) => {
      return await client.query({
        query,
        variables: {
          ...variables,
          [HeaderKeys.CacheUrl]: cacheUrl,  // Automatically added
        },
        ...
      });
    },
    url,
    host,
    ...
  });
}
```

* useStorefrontQuery Hook

```typescript theme={null}
// From: hooks/useStorefrontQuery.tsx

export function useStorefrontQuery(query, options) {
  const contextUrl = typeof window !== 'undefined' ? window.location.href : '';

  const mergedOptions = {
    ...options,
    variables: {
      [HeaderKeys.CacheUrl]: contextUrl,  // Automatically added
      ...options?.variables,
    },
    context: {
      ...options?.context,
      headers: {
        ...options?.context?.headers,
      },
    },
  };

  return useQuery(query, mergedOptions);
}
```

**Usage - No Manual Configuration Required**

* Using queryClient:

```typescript theme={null}
'use client';
import { queryClient } from 'services/dataService.client';

// x-litium-storefront-cache-url automatically added
const data = await queryClient({
  query: GET_CONTENT,
  variables: {
    category: 'electronics',
  },
});

// Variables sent:
// {
//   category: 'electronics',
//   x-litium-storefront-cache-url: 'https://example.com/products'  // Auto-injected
// }
```

* Using useStorefrontQuery:

```typescript theme={null}
'use client';
import { useStorefrontQuery } from 'hooks/useStorefrontQuery';

// x-litium-storefront-cache-url automatically added
const { data } = useStorefrontQuery(GET_CONTENT, {
  variables: {
    category: 'electronics',
  },
});

// Variables sent:
// {
//   x-litium-storefront-cache-url: 'https://example.com/products',  // Auto-injected (first)
//   category: 'electronics',
// }
```

## Mutating data in Server components

Use mutateServer for server-side mutations. from *services/dataService.server.ts*

**Function signature**

```typescript theme={null}
async function mutateServer(options: {
  mutation: DocumentNode;        // GraphQL mutation (required)
  client?: ApolloClient;         // Custom client (optional)
  url?: string;                  // Page URL (optional, defaults to headers)
  variables?: any;               // Mutation variables (optional)
}): Promise<any>
```

**Basic example**

```typescript theme={null}
'use server';
import { gql } from '@apollo/client';
import { redirect } from 'next/navigation';
import { mutateServer } from 'services/dataService.server';
import { get } from 'services/websiteService.server';
import { setCookieFromResponse } from 'utils/cookies';
import { getHost } from 'utils/headers';

export const signOutUser = async () => {
  const result = await mutateServer({
    mutation: SIGN_OUT_USER,
    variables: {},
  });
  return result;
};
```

## Mutating data in Client components

Use mutateClient for GraphQL mutations in Client Components. This is commonly used for cart operations, checkout, form submissions, etc.

**Function signature**

```typescript theme={null}
async function mutateClient(options: {
  client?: ApolloClient;         // Custom client (optional, defaults to global)
  mutation: DocumentNode;        // GraphQL mutation (required)
  url?: string;                  // Page URL (optional, defaults to window.location.pathname)
  host?: string;                 // Host (optional, defaults to window.location.host)
  variables?: any;               // Mutation variables (optional)
  context?: any;                 // Apollo context (optional)
}): Promise<any>
```

**Basic example**

```typescript theme={null}
import { gql } from '@apollo/client';
import { Cart } from 'models/cart';
import { mutateClient } from './dataService.client';

/**
 * Add a quantity of articleNumber to cart.
 */
export async function add(articleNumber: string, quantity = 1): Promise<Cart> {
  const data = await mutateClient({
    mutation: ADD,
    variables: {
      input: {
        articleNumber,
        quantity: +quantity,
      },
    },
  });
  return data;
}
```

## Summary

The Litium React accelerator provides four main methods for data operations:

1. `queryServer()` - Server-side queries (Server Components)
2. `useStorefrontQuery()` - Reactive client queries (Hook)
3. `queryClient()` - Imperative client queries (Function)
4. `mutateClient()` / `mutateServer()` - Mutations

## Folder structure

The project was created by using [create-next-app](https://nextjs.org/learn/dashboard-app/getting-started) tool and is pre-configured with Typescript, Tailwind, ESLint, Prettier, Jest and Playwright. All client resources are located in the src\client folder. It includes the following items:

app: NextJS's [app directory](https://beta.nextjs.org/docs/routing/fundamentals#the-app-directory) which was introduced in NextJS 13, which supports React Server Components.

components: React components.

e2e: End to end tests.

models: model interfaces.

operations: GraphQL's fragments and mutations.

public: static files like icons, images.

scripts: scripts to be used when building project.

services: service functions.

stores: state management's stores

styles: [Tailwind's base styles](https://tailwindcss.com/docs/preflight) and extensions.

utils: utility functions.

.env: [environment variables configuration](https://nextjs.org/docs/basic-features/environment-variables) file. For more information, please check [Get started](/accelerators/react-accelerator/get-started) page on how to set variables values.

tailwind.config.js: Tailwind's configuration file. To make it easier to override and extend stylings, the project is configured and using abstract color names and Tailwind's scale units. The theme then can be modified or extended by updating tailwind.config.js file. Please check [Theme configuration](https://tailwindcss.com/docs/theme) for more information.

# Routing fundamentals
Source: https://docs.litium.dev/accelerators/react-accelerator/routing-fundamentals

This page explains how to handle routing in React accelerator.

The routing in React accelerator is based on [NextJS's routing](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/building-your-application/routing) where files are defined in app directory to handle requests. The [Dynamic routes](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/building-your-application/routing/dynamic-routes) is used to handle requests for each page, product and category templates. For example:

* app/HomePage/\[\[...slug]]/page.tsx: handles requests to Home page template like [https://localhost:3001](https://localhost:3001), where the slug value is undefined, or [https://localhost:3001/another-home](https://localhost:3001/another-home) where the slug value is an array \[ another-home] .
* app/ProductWithVariantsProduct/\[\[...slug]]/page.tsx: handles requests to ProductWithVariants product template. For example: [https://localhost:3001/woman/tops/court-dress-black\_m-638113574893682732](https://localhost:3001/woman/tops/court-dress-black_m-638113574893682732), where the slug value is \[ 'woman', 'tops', 'court-dress-black\_m-638113574893682732' ]

## How does the system map an Url to a template?

Every pages, products and categories have a unique Url. This can be configured by setting the field Url.

<img alt="Litium URL field" />

When a request is made to this Url, a file named middleware.ts, which is a [NextJS's middleware](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/building-your-application/routing/middleware), is handling the incoming request. What the middleware does is, it sends a GraphQL request to Litium to get the template name of the Url, which is returned by the field \_\_typename. Then the request is forwared to the corresponsing page.tsx to handle. For example:

| URL                                                                                                                                                   | Template                   | Page file                                             |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- |
| [https://localhost:3001](https://localhost:3001)                                                                                                      | HomePage                   | app/HomePage/\[\[...slug]]/page.tsx                   |
| [https://localhost:3001/woman](https://localhost:3001/woman)                                                                                          | CategoryProductCategory    | app/CategoryProductCategory/\[\[...slug]]/page.tsx    |
| [https://localhost:3001/woman/tops/court-dress-black\_m-638113574893682732](https://localhost:3001/woman/tops/court-dress-black_m-638113574893682732) | ProductWithVariantsProduct | app/ProductWithVariantsProduct/\[\[...slug]]/page.tsx |

At the end of middleware.ts, there is a [Matcher](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/building-your-application/routing/middleware#matcher) config to config what requests are ignored by the middleware.

# Settings
Source: https://docs.litium.dev/accelerators/react-accelerator/settings

In the website fields template, there are pointer fields designated to set up the URL for the pages, which are then utilized to retrieve pages in the React accelerator.

<img alt="Website fields template" />

* **Field group Search: Search result page**: The page where the user ends up after performing a search
* **Field group Order confirmation page: Order confirmation page**: The page that will be displayed as order confirmation page
* **Field group Errors: Page not found (404)**: The pointed out page will be shown to users when a page is not found.
* **General error (500)**: The pointed out page will be shown to users when the system returns a general 500-error

<Note>
  In a 500 error page, only the title and information about the error are displayed, no blocks are displayed.
</Note>


# Upgrading Tailwind CSS to v4
Source: https://docs.litium.dev/accelerators/react-accelerator/upgrade-guide-for-tailwindcss-4

This document provides a comprehensive guide for upgrading your Tailwind CSS installation from v3 to v4.

## 1: Use the Official Upgrade Tool

Start with the automated upgrade tool:

```bash theme={null}
npx @tailwindcss/upgrade
```

## 2: Breaking Changes

**2.1. SCSS Removal (Required)**

Tailwind v4 uses Lightning CSS for nested CSS, and is not intended to be used with preprocessors like Sass. If your Sass files are only used for nested selectors, you can:

* Rename .scss/.sass files to .css
* Keep the nested selector syntax — Lightning CSS will process it correctly
* Update any import paths or build config references from .scss to .css

**2.2. Theme configuration moved into CSS (migration to CSS variables)**

JavaScript config files are no longer detected automatically in v4; theme configuration now lives in a CSS file (*styles/theme.css*) using the @theme directive and CSS variables.

What to do:

* Remove or archive *tailwind.config.js*.
* Create *styles/theme.css* and declare your theme using @theme and CSS variables
* Replace uses of custom theme tokens in your project to reference the new CSS variables where necessary (or rely on Tailwind utility classes if they are generated by the new @theme usage).

**2.3 Custom breakpoint class removal / new pointer classes**

Tailwind v4 provides pointer-aware utilities. Replace old custom names as follows:

* `hoverable` becomes `pointer-fine`
* `touchable` becomes `pointer-coarse`

Search and update class usage across templates and components.

**2.4 Renamed custom utility classnames**

Update these custom class names:

* `bg-disabled-background` becomes `bg-disabled`
* `border-disabled-border` becomes `border-disabled`

Search and replace these strings across templates, components, styles, and tests.

## References

* [Official upgrade guide](https://tailwindcss.com/docs/upgrade-guide)


# Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG)
Source: https://docs.litium.dev/accelerators/react-accelerator/web-content-accessibility-guidelines

The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG), developed by the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C), provide a shared international standard for web accessibility. The React accelerator is designed to be compliant with the WCAG 2.2 Level AA standard.

To better comply with the EU Accessibility Act the Litium accelerator supports most of the necessary changes to comply with [WCAG 2.2 AA](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/quickref/). Below are some things added to enhance accessibility.

* Enhanced ARIA attributes for core elements, including navigation, sidebars, modals, dropdowns, checkboxes, accordions, images, and icons.
* Keyboard navigation support is implemented for all complex and interactive components.
* Improved form accessibility using autocomplete and dedicated ARIA attributes for better input handling.
* Utilized Landmarks to clearly define page regions for screen reader navigation.
* Implemented skip links to allow users to bypass menus and jump directly to main content.
* Utilized semantically appropriate `<Button>` elements across various components for improved accessibility.
* Implemented a color scheme that ensures enhanced contrast for improved readability.
* Focus styles are clearly defined and visible to aid keyboard users.
* Ensured consistent component usage throughout the application for a reliable user experience.
* Integrated the jsx-a11y ESLint plugin for static accessibility checks in the codebase.

## Best practices

To ensure your solution complies with WCAG 2.2 AA, here are our recommendations:

* Use built-in components of the React accelerator.
* For custom page templates and components, use these tools to check for compliance:
  * ESLint: for static code analysis.
  * [Axe DevTools extension](https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/axe-devtools-web-accessib/lhdoppojpmngadmnindnejefpokejbdd).
  * [Chrome Lighthouse accessibility](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/lighthouse/accessibility/scoring) tool.
  * [BrowserStack Accessibility testing](https://www.browserstack.com/docs/accessibility).

# Products block
Source: https://docs.litium.dev/accelerators/react-accelerator/working-with-blocks/products-block

The products block is suited for displaying a selection of products on pages of your website. Products to show can be selected from a category or a product list.

The product block has the following fields:

| Field              | Type        | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| ------------------ | ----------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Name               | Text        | The name of the block                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| Title              | Text        | The title of the block                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| Category           | Pointer     | Category to display products from                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| Product list       | Pointer     | Product list to display products from. Will only be used if no category is selected.                                                                                                                              |
| Number of products | Integer     | Number of products to display. If no value is entered, a default number of 15 products will be displayed. A maximum number of 100 products will be displayed.                                                     |
| Sorting            | Text option | Possible values: Recommended or Popular. Recommended will display only products from the selected category, not sub-categories. Popular will display products from the selected category including subcategories. |


# Working with Google Analytics and Google Tag Manager
Source: https://docs.litium.dev/accelerators/react-accelerator/working-with-google-tag-manager

This page is an introduction to how to work with Google Analytics and Google Tag Manager.

## How to configure Google Tag Manager

Create an account and container in [Google Tag Manager](https://support.google.com/tagmanager/answer/14842164?hl=en).

Find your GTM container ID in the Workspace tab of the Tag Manager panel.

<img alt="GTM container ID" />

Login to Litium and go to **Settings > Globalization > Channels**. Select your channel, and in the **Settings** tab, enter the GTM container ID into the "Google Tag Manager Container ID (GTM)" field.

<Note>
  In React accelerator, only this field is used to configure GTM, while the other fields are used on the MVC accelerator.
</Note>

<img alt="Channel GTM settings" />

Here is the code to query GTM container ID in *websiteService.server.ts* file from Storefront API.

```graphql theme={null}
query GetWebsite {
    channel {
      ... on DefaultChannelFieldTemplateChannel {
        analytics {
          googleTagManager
        }
      }
    }
}
```

In the React accelerator, third-party Google services for Next.js are implemented. After configuring the GTM container ID in the TrackingManager component and including it in the layout, the service automatically generates and injects the GTM script during setup.

## Configure Google Analytics through Google Tag Manager

**Google Analytics** (GA) is implemented and managed exclusively through Google Tag Manager (GTM). GTM acts as the intermediary platform that manages all GA tags, triggers, and variables required for data collection and reporting.

* **No Direct GA Code Implementation**: There is no standalone or hardcoded GA script in the application.
* **Centralized Tag Management**: All configurations, including page views, events, and custom dimensions/metrics, are controlled via GTM.

Here is a guide to [configure Google Analytics in Tag Manager](https://support.google.com/tagmanager/answer/9442095?hl=en).

## How to send custom events?

To send custom events, use the trackEvent function in the *TrackingManager.tsx* component. Here is an example:

```tsx theme={null}
trackEvent({ event: 'MyTest', value: 'hello-world' })
```


# Article page
Source: https://docs.litium.dev/accelerators/react-accelerator/working-with-page-types/article-page

The article page type is suited for the editorial content of your storefront, eg product guides, contact information and blog posts.

The article page has the following fields:

| Field                           | Type         | Description                                                                                          |
| ------------------------------- | ------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Name                            | Text         | The name of the page, used in the left menu                                                          |
| URL                             | Text         | The URL of the page                                                                                  |
| Show navigation for child pages | Boolean      | if set to true, the left menu will display a tree structure for any child pages of the current page. |
| Title                           | Text         | The title of the page, used as the header when the page is displayed                                 |
| Introduction                    | MultirowText | Short introduction to the contents of the page                                                       |
| Text                            | Editor       | The content of the page                                                                              |

The article page has one block container.
